name: Voxel Cube World
summary: A bright MagicaVoxel-style miniature world: every actor is a real 3D cube grid, baked to sprites under one warm afternoon sun.
description: Characters, props, pickups, particles and even HUD icons are small 3D voxel grids that a tiny software renderer turns into sprites once at startup: 3/4 orthographic view at 46 degrees, three face tones, per-voxel colour jitter and ambient occlusion. The ground is a flat field of 4x4-unit voxel tiles with one-voxel height steps whose side faces and lit edges show, plus blocky blurred sun shadows. It reads like a tabletop toy diorama: saturated autumn colours, chunky shapes, no outlines.
avoidFor: games needing many free-rotating 3D camera angles

difficulty.why: New models are 3D cube grids that can be described very precisely in code; the renderer does the light and shadow automatically.

technique.renderer: Canvas 2D (procedural, no image assets) with a built-in software voxel renderer that bakes sprites at init
technique.resolution: Native resolution. Sprites are baked at K = round(screenH/360*4)/4 (clamped 1.5–4) sprite px per world unit, with PPV = max(3, round(K*1.9)) px per voxel, so one voxel is ~1.9–2 world units. Ground chunks are rendered per pixel at up to 2.5 px per unit; blits are snapped to whole screen pixels.
technique.summary: Every object is a Uint16 voxel grid (x right, y toward the viewer, z up). At init each grid is rotated by a yaw (±0.6 rad for characters), projected orthographically with a 46° pitch, its exposed faces sorted back-to-front and filled as quads with 3 tones, jitter and AO, giving MagicaVoxel-looking sprites for 2 facings × all animation frames.
technique.linework: No outlines at all. Form is separated purely by face tones (top 1.0, sun-facing side ~0.88, shadow side ~0.68) and by dark 'carved' voxels painted on the front surface (e.g. #8a3412 rim around a glowing face). Faces are grown by 0.8 sprite px to hide hairline seams.
technique.shading: Three flat face tones per voxel: top = 1.0 and warmed (r×1.035, g×1.015, b×0.965); side tone = 0.76 − 0.15 × (screen-x of the rotated normal), so the left-facing side is ~0.88 and the right-facing side ~0.68, and sides are cooled toward blue. Each voxel's brightness is jittered ±4.5% by a hash. Each solid neighbour around an open face subtracts 7.5% (AO); side faces of the bottom layer get ×0.9.
technique.lighting: One fixed warm sun from the upper left (west). Cast shadows are blocky footprints sheared by (0.62, 0.26) per unit of height toward the lower right, blurred 0.16×PPV px, drawn at 42% alpha. Emissive voxels (carved faces, cracks, eyes, lamps) skip shading and get an additive radial glow sprite. A purple radial vignette and a faint warm top gradient finish the frame.
technique.texture: No texture maps. Variation comes from per-voxel hash jitter, random colour picks per voxel inside a material (2–4 shades), and on the ground per-tile colour picks from 4–7 shades plus a 1-px lit/dark tile bevel.

paletteRules: Bright, saturated mid-tones only: no pure black anywhere in the world; the darkest world colours are carved/hole voxels (#1c2044, #24122c, #2c221e).
Every material is 2–4 close shades picked per voxel by a hash, never one flat colour.
Warm sunlit tops, cool bluish sides: shading shifts hue, not just brightness.
Glowing parts (faces, cracks, eyes, lamps) are emissive voxels in yellow/orange plus an additive glow; they are the only things that glow.
Enemies are purple/white against a green/grey/brown world; the hero is orange + navy + teal so it pops on every ground type.
UI uses a separate dark-purple family (#2b2446 / #151024) with gold text so it never blends into the bright world.

background.summary: A flat infinite voxel terrain baked per 256-unit chunk, pixel by pixel: 4×4-unit tiles, each with a material (grass, leaf litter, field, stone, path, water) and a height (-1 water, 0 field/path, 1 normal, 2 raised). Where the tile to the north is higher, its side face is painted into the top of the lower tile, so the world looks like a stepped voxel diorama seen from above.
layers: Base: per-tile colour from the material's shade list (noise + hash pick), ×(0.95–1.05) macro brightness noise
Tile bevel: top/left 0.42-unit strip ×1.035/×1.015, bottom/right ×0.95/×0.965 (stone joints ×0.86 / ×1.05)

Height steps: lit top edge (north colour ×1.14 + 6), grass lip (×0.8, 1.05 units), side face band of 1.9 units per height step in the material's side colour fading ×0.98→0.78, then a 0.9-unit contact shadow ×0.84
Sun shadow of west neighbours: 1.5-unit strip ×0.8 on lower tiles east of a higher tile
Decals on a 7-unit jittered grid: tiny voxel grass tufts, flowers, pebbles, leaves, twigs, sprouts, cracks, lily pads, reeds (each a 2-rect mini cube with its own shadow)
Per frame: blinking water glints (#e8f8ff), a warm additive light pool under the hero

characters.summary: Characters are voxel grids of roughly 10×9×18 voxels (hero), built from boxes and super-ellipsoid blobs, with faces painted onto the front-most voxel of each column. Each grid is baked for yaw +0.6 (facing right) and -0.6 (facing left) and for every animation frame (hero: idle + 4 walk, enemies: 4), so the 3D model really turns instead of being mirrored.
rules: Big head, short body: the hero's pumpkin head is 10×9×8 voxels on a 6-voxel body; enemies are mostly one big blob with tiny legs.
Animation is done by rebuilding the grid per frame: legs shift ±1 voxel in y, the body lifts 1 voxel, arms counter-swing, leaves sway ±1 voxel.
Faces are 1-voxel pixels on the front surface: emissive yellow for friendly glow, emissive red eyes and dark brows for enemies, dark holes for ghosts.
Each actor has one dominant colour family and a contrasting light underside (cream, white) so silhouettes read on any ground.
No outlines and no mirroring; separate yaw renders keep the light from the left on both facings.
Every actor casts a blocky blurred shadow to the lower right (alpha 0.42; floating actors 0.22).

effects.name: Cube debris
effects.how: Hits and kills spawn 2–34 tiny 1-voxel cubes (pre-rendered in 6 yaw frames at 2K px per unit, no AO) in the victim's palette; they fly with vz 60–140, gravity 320, drag 1.4, tumble through the 6 frames and leave a small square shadow when on the ground.

effects.name: Square rings
effects.how: Shockwaves are axis-aligned rectangles squashed by sin(46°) (strokeRect), radius easing outQuad 10→48 units, line width 3·k+0.4, alpha 0.85·k, colours #fff1c8 / #ffd84a – never circles.

effects.name: Layered spawn
effects.how: Enemies rise out of the ground: the sprite is cropped from the bottom and revealed in whole voxel layers (PPV·cos46° px) while 4 dirt cubes pop around them.

effects.name: Hit flash and death squash
effects.how: A white silhouette copy (source-atop tint) at alpha ≤0.58; on death the sprite scales x 1+0.35t, y 1−0.6t over 0.28 s with a fading white overlay, then cubes burst.

effects.name: Emissive bloom
effects.how: Additive (lighter) radial gradient sprite (0.9 → 0.35 → 0 alpha) over carved faces (alpha 0.34 ± 0.06 flicker at 9 rad/s), lamps, lanterns and brute cracks.

effects.name: Seed projectile trail
effects.how: A spinning 3×2×4 voxel seed with three trailing squares 3.2 units apart, sizes 1.75/1.3/0.85, alphas 0.41/0.27/0.13 in #fff6dc / #ffe2a8.

effects.name: Pickups
effects.how: Stepped voxel octahedra in 8 spin frames, hovering 2.4 ± 0.9 units, with a mint (or gold for big) additive glow and a flat dark square shadow.

ui.summary: Chunky 'voxel slab' UI: flat dark-purple panels with a 3 px near-black edge, a hard 6 px drop edge below and inset hard highlights/shadows instead of gradients. Bars are segmented with 3 px dark gaps every 18 px and have 3 hard colour bands (highlight / main / shade). Bungee numbers carry stacked hard drop shadows that look extruded; icons are the same voxel models rendered at icon size.

motion: Hero walk: 4 baked frames (plus 1 idle), frame = 1 + floor(anim·1.6) mod 4; idle hops up to 0.6 units with max(0, sin(t·2.6)).
Small enemy: 4 frames at anim·1.8; brute: 4 frames at anim·1.3; ghost: 4 frames at 6 fps, floats 2.5 ± 1.5 units (sin t·2.8) at alpha 0.84.
Pickups spin through 8 yaw frames (1.6 turns of the set per second) and bob ±0.9 units at 3 rad/s; orbiting lanterns pick their spin frame from the orbit angle and hover 9 ± 1.2 units.
All motion is stepped by whole frames and blits are snapped to screen pixels – nothing rotates or scales smoothly except death squash and particles.
Glows flicker with small sines (±0.02–0.12 alpha at 4–11 rad/s); water glints blink when sin(t·1.7 + phase) > 0.55.
Damage numbers pop 0.6→1.15 scale in the first 12% of life, then settle; crits get a '!' and gold colour.
do: Model everything — props, pickups, particles, icons — as voxel grids and bake them through the same renderer so lighting is identical.
Keep one voxel ≈ 2 world units and the hero ≈ 10 voxels wide so all assets share one cube size.
Bake two yaws (±0.6 rad) per character instead of mirroring, so the sun stays on the left.
Use 2–4 hashed shades per material and the ±4.5% per-voxel jitter; it is what makes it look like MagicaVoxel.
Paint faces and markings onto the front-most voxel (paintFront) and use emissive colours plus an additive glow for anything that should shine.
Give every object the blocky sheared sun shadow to the lower right.
Make the ground out of 4×4-unit tiles with visible 1-voxel steps and lit edges.
dont: Don't add outlines or black strokes – voxel faces define the forms.
Don't use smooth gradients or soft round shapes on actors; only glows and the vignette are soft.
Don't rotate or scale baked sprites at runtime (except death squash) – re-bake a new yaw/frame instead.
Don't mix voxel sizes: a 1-unit-voxel prop next to 2-unit-voxel characters breaks the miniature scale.
Don't use circular rings or round particles; effects are square rings and little cubes.
Don't light from multiple directions or add dynamic light to the ground beyond a faint warm pool.
Don't use muted/dark palettes for the world; the look depends on bright, sunlit toy colours.
performance: All voxel rendering happens once in init(): ~5 hero frames + 3×4 enemy frames × 2 yaws, 8-frame spin sets, ~15 props, 1-voxel debris cubes in 6 frames and shadows — a few hundred ms at most. Per frame everything is plain drawImage of cached canvases (tinted flash copies are cached per frame/colour). The expensive part is the ground: per-pixel chunk rendering with several noise calls per tile, done as a generator over multiple frames; on-screen cost is just chunk blits. Big hordes are cheap because each enemy is 2–3 drawImage calls.
